---
title: "🧭 Topics"
subtitle: "What the course covers, and which method answers which question"
---

The course is built in four blocks. Each block is a stage in the same chain of
reasoning: what a molecule *is*, what we can *do* to it, what a genome *says*,
and what any of that lets us *claim* about an ecological system.

# The four blocks

::: {.dropdown-table}

<details open>
<summary><strong>Block I</strong> — Foundations and measurement</summary>

- evolution, scientific reasoning, and molecular biology as a way of knowing;
- chemical properties of DNA, RNA, proteins, buffers, enzymes, and molecular interactions;
- information flow: replication, mutation, repair, recombination, transcription, translation, and regulation;
- sample representativeness, preservation, extraction, quantification, inhibition, and contamination.

*Weeks 1–2, and the practical block in weeks 14–16. Slides:*
[Introduction](lectures/introduction.html) ·
[The code of life](lectures/code_of_life.html)

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Block II</strong> — The molecular toolkit</summary>

- electrophoresis, restriction analysis, Southern blotting, PCR, qPCR, ddPCR, Sanger sequencing, probes, FISH, fluorescence, and flow cytometry;
- molecular markers: barcoding, metabarcoding, allozymes, RFLP, microsatellites, and SNPs;
- Illumina, PacBio, Oxford Nanopore, library preparation, read quality, assembly, annotation, and data management.

*Weeks 3–6. Slides:*
[The molecular toolkit](lectures/lecture2.html) ·
[Sequencing technologies](lectures/lecture3.html) ·
[Markers and DNA sources](lectures/loeng4.html) ·
[eDNA and hybridization](lectures/loeng5.html)

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Block III</strong> — Genomes and molecular phenotypes</summary>

- comparative genomics, assembly, annotation, and public sequence databases;
- transcriptomics, non-coding RNA, condition- and stage-specific regulation, epigenetics, and functional genomics;
- proteomics, quantitative proteomics, protein interactions, post-translational modification, and molecular phenotypes;
- the cell biology behind the traits we measure: life-cycle stages, secretion, transport, and cellular responses to the environment.

*Weeks 7–9.*

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Block IV</strong> — Ecology, evolution, and application</summary>

- phylogeny, phylogeography, population genetics, coalescence, and community-level inference;
- species interactions, symbiosis, host-associated microbiota, and environmental monitoring;
- CRISPR, LAMP, microfluidics, lab-on-chip, biosensing, and field-deployable diagnostics.

*Weeks 10–12.*

</details>

:::

# Which method for which question

A method is only as good as the question it is asked to answer. This table is
the one to argue with in seminars.

| The question | Typical approach | The thing that usually goes wrong |
|---|---|---|
| Is this species present here? | Targeted qPCR or ddPCR assay on eDNA | Assay specificity; a positive means *DNA was present*, not *the animal was* |
| What is in this community? | Metabarcoding of a marker region | Primer bias and reference-database gaps decide what you can possibly detect |
| What is this specimen? | Sanger barcoding of COI, ITS, 16S/18S | The reference sequence may be misidentified; barcode gaps vary by group |
| How are these populations connected? | Microsatellites, SNP panels, RAD-seq | Sampling design, not marker count, limits the inference |
| What is the evolutionary history? | Multi-locus phylogeny, coalescent models | Gene trees are not species trees |
| What is this organism doing right now? | Transcriptomics, RT-qPCR, eRNA | RNA degradation and the sampling instant dominate the signal |
| How much biomass or how many cells? | Flow cytometry, qPCR standard curves | Calibration and gating decisions carry most of the uncertainty |
| What did this ecosystem look like before? | Sedimentary and ancient DNA | Damage, contamination, and leaching between layers |
| Which genes are present in this genome? | Assembly and annotation | Assembly errors propagate silently into every downstream count |

# Skills you should leave with

::: {.dropdown-table}

<details>
<summary><strong>At the bench</strong></summary>

- extract nucleic acids from environmental, tissue, faecal, sediment, or low-biomass material and say why you chose that protocol;
- design a PCR with the controls that make its result interpretable: extraction blank, no-template control, positive control, technical replicates, inhibition check;
- read an agarose gel, a Sanger trace, a qPCR amplification curve, and a standard curve;
- keep a notebook another person could use to repeat what you did.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>At the keyboard</strong></summary>

- assess FASTQ quality and a Nanopore run report, and decide whether the data are usable;
- run a barcoding or metabarcoding workflow from reads to a taxon table;
- build and read a phylogenetic tree, and state what the support values do and do not mean;
- produce a reproducible report that keeps observation, analysis, inference, and speculation visibly separate.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>In an argument</strong></summary>

- compare Sanger, short-read, and long-read sequencing for a stated objective and defend the choice on cost, error profile, and read length;
- identify the step in someone else's study where the inference actually becomes fragile;
- state the limitations of your own design before a reviewer does.

</details>

:::
